title: Target Heart Rate Calculator: how it works, formula and examples

content:
The [Target Heart Rate Calculator](/target-heart-rate-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Your training heart-rate zones — Karvonen zones from age and resting heart rate. Enter your age and resting heart rate (bpm) and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Find your training heart-rate zones with the Karvonen method: your maximum heart rate is estimated from your age (Tanaka: 208 − 0.7 × age), your heart-rate reserve is the gap between that maximum and your resting rate, and each training zone is a percentage of that reserve added back to your resting rate. The result is more personal than a plain percentage of maximum, because two people with the same maximum but different resting rates get different zones. These zones are a guide for exercise — stop and seek medical advice if you feel chest pain, dizziness or unusual breathlessness.

## How to use the Target Heart Rate Calculator

Start by entering your age, then entering your resting heart rate (bpm). The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Enter your age.
2. Enter your resting heart rate — morning, lying down, before coffee.
3. Read your maximum heart rate and the four training zones.
4. Train in the zone that matches your goal: moderate for endurance, vigorous for fitness gains.

## Formula

HRmax = 208 − 0.7 × age. Heart rate reserve = HRmax − resting HR. Target = resting HR + reserve × intensity (50–60% light, 60–70% moderate, 70–85% vigorous, 85–95% peak).

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Target Heart Rate Calculator](/target-heart-rate-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. A 30-year-old with a resting heart rate of 60: maximum is 187 bpm and the reserve is 127. The moderate zone (60–70%) is 136–149 bpm, and the vigorous zone (70–85%) is 149–168 bpm. Try the same figures in the [Target Heart Rate Calculator](/target-heart-rate-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Age: 30, Resting heart rate (bpm): 60), the [Target Heart Rate Calculator](/target-heart-rate-calculator) returns Maximum heart rate: 187 bpm, Heart rate reserve: 127 bpm, Light zone (50–60%): 124–136 bpm, Moderate zone (60–70%): 136–149 bpm, Vigorous zone (70–85%): 149–168 bpm, Peak zone (85–95%): 168–181 bpm. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [BMI Calculator](/bmi-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## What each zone is for

The light zone (50–60%) is warm-up, recovery and easy walking. The moderate zone (60–70%) is where most endurance training happens — you can talk in full sentences and sustain it for an hour. The vigorous zone (70–85%) is hard tempo and interval work, where fitness improves fastest. The peak zone (85–95%) is short, very hard efforts for trained athletes. Most of a week's training should be in the light and moderate zones, with only one or two hard sessions.

## Karvonen vs percentage of maximum

A plain percentage of maximum heart rate ignores your resting rate, so it gives the same zones to a fit person (resting 50) and an unfit one (resting 80) of the same age. Karvonen uses the reserve — the range your heart actually works across — so the zones sit lower for the fit person and higher for the unfit one, matching how hard the effort feels. That is why coaches prefer it.

## Limits of the estimate

Maximum heart rate is estimated from age, and the estimate can be off by 10 beats or more for an individual — some people's true maximum is much higher or lower than the formula. Heart-rate medication, illness and heat also change the numbers. Use the zones as a guide, and pay attention to how the effort feels: if you cannot speak in the moderate zone, you are going too hard whatever the watch says.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Measure resting heart rate over several mornings and average it — a single reading can mislead by 5 bpm.
- Keep most training easy: about 80% of weekly time in the light and moderate zones.
- If you take heart-rate medication, ask your doctor what zones apply to you.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the Karvonen formula?

Target heart rate = resting heart rate + (maximum heart rate − resting heart rate) × intensity. It uses your heart-rate reserve, so the zones reflect your own fitness rather than just your age. You can see it in action in the [Target Heart Rate Calculator](/target-heart-rate-calculator) — enter your own values and the result updates as you type.

### What heart rate should I exercise at?

For general fitness, most of your exercise should be in the moderate zone (60–70% of reserve), where you can still talk. Short vigorous sessions (70–85%) build fitness faster but need recovery days. Try it with your own numbers in the [Target Heart Rate Calculator](/target-heart-rate-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is a good resting heart rate?

For most adults, 60–100 bpm at rest is considered normal, and trained athletes are often 40–60. A resting rate that climbs over weeks can signal illness, stress or overtraining. Try it with your own numbers in the [Target Heart Rate Calculator](/target-heart-rate-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What do I need to use the Target Heart Rate Calculator?

Just Age and Resting heart rate (bpm). Enter those values and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. If you are unsure about a value, try a rough figure first and then refine it — the result updates instantly.
